sec.title: Background
sec.p: The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) recently endorsed low-dose colchicine for chronic coronary syndrome. However, its role in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains uncertain due to inconsistent trial outcomes. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of colchicine in patients with ACS.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted through April 2025 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating colchicine in adults with ACS. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular mortality, stroke, myocardial infarction (MI), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), coronary revascularization, and gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events. Data were pooled using a random-effects model to estimate relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), using the longest available follow-up.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Eleven RCTs encompassing 12,730 patients were included. Among them, 6,844 received colchicine for at least one month, while 5,886 received placebo or no additional treatment. Colchicine did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality (RR 0.95, 95% CI: 0.79–1.14) or cardiovascular mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI: 0.82–1.29). No significant reductions were observed in MACE, MI, stroke, or coronary revascularization. Colchicine was associated with a non-significant trend toward increased GI adverse events, particularly at higher doses.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis does not support the routine use of colchicine in ACS management. While generally safe, colchicine did not confer clear cardiovascular benefits in this setting. However, potential subgroup effects, such as in longer-term use or among specific high-risk populations, warrant further investigation in future large-scale, well-designed trials.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Despite advancements in treatment over the last few decades, acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide [1]. Standard therapies, such as revascularization, antithrombotic regimens, cholesterol-lowering medications, and antianginal drugs, have significantly improved clinical outcomes in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) [2–4]. ACS mostly results from acute thrombus formation due to plaque rupture or erosion, whereas chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) involves stable atherosclerotic plaques causing exertional ischemia from a fixed flow limitation [5]. While ACS presents abruptly with high infarction risk, CCS reflects a more gradual disease course.

Inflammation plays a key role in the development and progression of atherosclerosis, making it a critical factor in ACS [6]. In recent years, anti-inflammatory treatments have gained attention as potential therapeutic options [7]. However, many of these drugs pose safety concerns in cardiac settings. For instance, Canakinumab, an interleukin-1β inhibitor, has been shown to reduce ischemic events in post-myocardial infarction (MI) patients but also increases the risk of fatal infections, highlighting the need for safer alternatives [8].

Colchicine, a low-cost, cardiac-safe, anti-inflammatory drug, has been used for decades in managing gout, pericarditis, and Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) [9, 10]. Its anti-inflammatory effects are achieved through multiple mechanisms, including inhibition of neutrophil activity and suppression of inflammatory chemokines such as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 [11, 12]. Given its safety profile and anti-inflammatory properties, colchicine has been recommended by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) for patients with CCS [13]. However, its potential benefits in ACS remain uncertain.

Several clinical trials have examined colchicine’s role in cardiovascular care, yielding mixed results. In patients with ACS, the recently published CLEAR SYNERGY trial found that while colchicine reduced C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, it did not significantly lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) over a median follow-up of three years [14].

To clarify colchicine’s role in ACS, we conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate its efficacy and safety in patients with ACS based on data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The current study is in accordance with the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis protocols (PRISMA, See Supplementary Materials) [15]. Our systematic review and meta‐analysis protocol has been registered at Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD42024623443).

sec.title: Search strategy and eligibility criteria
sec.p: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to April 12, 2025, without restriction on language or study type. Search terms included combinations of “colchicine,” “myocardial infarction,” and “acute coronary syndrome,” using appropriate Boolean operators (See Supplementary Materials). Furthermore, we carefully reviewed the reference lists of review articles, meta-analyses, and original studies identified through the search to identify potentially relevant studies.

Following the exclusion of duplicates, 4 independent investigators (A.A., D.N., F.J., F.M.) reviewed the titles and abstracts of the search results and discrepancies were resolved through mutual consensus. Our inclusion criteria were as follows: [1] RCTs with at least one month of active follow-up during the trial phase; [2] investigating colchicine as the intervention, regardless of type, dosage, or route of administration; [3] enrolling adults diagnosed with ACS, including ST-elevation MI (STEMI), non-ST elevation MI (NSTEMI), and unstable angina; [4] using placebo or standard care as the comparator; and [5] reporting relevant clinical outcomes. We excluded studies that focused solely on peri-procedural phase to ensure our analysis addressed broader treatment outcomes and did not focus only on the period surrounding the percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) procedure. Observational studies, case reports, conference abstracts, reviews, and studies without clear outcome measures were excluded.

sec.title: Data extraction and outcomes
sec.p: Four independent authors (F.M., P.P., F.J., A.A.) extracted data on study characteristics, participants’ characteristics, and clinical outcomes from the eligible studies onto a dedicated spreadsheet. Extracted variables included first author, publication year, country, study design, sample size, population characteristics, colchicine dose and duration, follow-up time, and outcome definitions. We obtained the outcomes for the longest available follow-up. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), recurrent MI, stroke, need for revascularization, and adverse gastrointestinal (GI) events. Where outcome definitions varied across studies, we adopted the definitions used in each trial and noted the differences. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and mutual consensus.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration’s Risk of Bias-2 (RoB‐2) tool [16], which examines key domains such as randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and the selection of the reported result. Bias risk was classified as low, high, or some concern. The quality assessment was independently performed by two authors (A.A. and M.F.) using predefined criteria. Any disagreements regarding the quality evaluation were resolved through discussion with a third author (P.F.). Moreover, the quality of evidence for each outcome parameter was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) framework [17].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.1.2 (The R Foundation, Vienna, Austria) to assess the risk ratios (RR) for various outcomes. A random-effects meta-analysis using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) method was applied to calculate pooled RR along with their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup analyses were conducted based on colchicine dose and duration of intervention (1 month as short-term, more than 1 month as long-term). Heterogeneity across studies was evaluated using the Q-statistic and I² statistics, with heterogeneity levels classified as low (< 30%), moderate (30–60%), or high (> 60%). Sensitivity analysis was performed using the leave-one-out method. Publication bias was assessed using Begg’s test. Funnel plots were performed only for all-cause mortality, as there were fewer than 10 studies for the other outcomes. The analysis utilized the meta, metafor, readxl, dplyr, tidyverse, and ggplot2 libraries. Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05.

sec.title: Search results
sec.p: A systematic literature search identified 3,095 articles, with 2,283 remaining after duplicates were removed. Following the full-text screening, 105 unique studies were assessed for eligibility, and 11 RCTs met the inclusion criteria (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: The included studies encompass populations with ACS subtypes, including STEMI, NSTEMI, and unstable angina. The intervention group comprised 6,844 participants receiving colchicine, while the control group included 5,886 participants receiving either a placebo (7 studies) or no additional treatment (4 studies) in conjunction with standard ACS management. Raju et al. included patients with ACS or acute ischemic stroke. For this meta-analysis, we only used data pertaining to ACS patients [18]. The duration of the follow-up varied from one month to three years, during which patients remained on the intervention. Colchicine doses ranged from 0.5 mg once daily to 1 mg once daily. Two studies, COLCOT [19] and CLEAR SYNERGY [14], were multinational, with CLEAR SYNERGY reporting the longest follow-up of 3 years. Charectristics of included RCTs are presented in Table 1 and Supplemntal Table 1. The mean age of participants across the included studies ranged from approximately 55 to 61 years, with majority participants being male. Details on baseline characteristics of included particpants are provided in Table 2.

sec.title: Quality assesment
sec.p: Three studies were classified as having a low risk of bias, and eight studies had some concerns (See Fig. 2). The quality of evidence was rated as high to moderate for most outcomes, with downgrades mainly due to wide confidence intervals and substantial heterogeneity (See Supplemental Table 2).

sec.title: Mortality
sec.p: All-cause mortality was reported in 10 studies. Although colchicine was associated with a slightly lower risk compared to standard ACS treatment alone, the reduction was not statistically significant (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.79–1.14; I² = 0.0%, p = 0.56; Fig. 3). The results remained consistent in the sensitivity analysis (See Supplemental Fig. 1). Similarly, colchicine showed no significant effect on cardiovascular mortality as reported in 8 studies (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.82–1.29, I² = 0.0%, p = 0.81; Fig. 4), with no significant differences in the sensitivity analysis (See Supplemental Fig. 2).

sec.title: Major adverse cardiac events
sec.p: Regarding MACE in 5 studies, no significant reduction was observed with colchicine treatment (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.43–1.17, I² = 64.4%, p = 0.13; Supplemental Fig. 3), with no significant differences observed in the sensitivity analysis (Supplemental Fig. 4).

sec.title: Myocardial infarction, stroke, and coronary revascularization
sec.p: Although the point estimates favored colchicine, there was no significant effect on the incidence of MI (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.73–1.05, I² = 0.0%, p = 0.15; Supplemental Fig. 5) or revascularization (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.32–1.18, I² = 70.7%, p = 0.15; Supplemental Fig. 6). Similarly, the risk of stroke did not differ significantly between the colchicine and control groups (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.23–1.36, I² = 57.0%, p = 0.21; Supplemental Fig. 7). Sensitivity analysis (Supplemental Figs. 8–10) revealed that excluding the study of Jolly et al. [14] significantly reduced the risk of revascularization (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.72), and the risk of stroke (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.14–0.67).

sec.title: Gastrointestinal adverse events
sec.p: Colchicine treatment was not associated with a significantly higher risk of GI adverse events (RR 1.51, 95% CI 0.96–2.38, I² = 78.0%, p = 0.6; Supplemental Fig. 11), however, excluding the studies by Tardif [17] resulted in a significantly higher risk of GI adverse events (Supplemental Fig. 12). Subgroup analysis revealed that 1 mg daily colchicine was associated with significantly higher incidence of GI adverse events (RR 11.93, 95% CI 1.59–89.71, I² = 0.0%; Supplemental Fig. 13).

sec.title: Publication bias
sec.p: There was no evidence of publication bias, as indicated by Begg’s test (p > 0.05) (Supplemental Fig. 14).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs demonstrated that colchicine showed neutral clinical outcomes in patients with ACS. No meaningful differences were observed between colchicine and either placebo or standard treatment alone regarding, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MACE, MI, revascularization, or stroke.

Colchicine has been proposed as a potential therapeutic agent for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease due to its anti-inflammatory mechanisms [27]. By inhibiting microtubule elongation and polymerization, colchicine suppresses neutrophil activation and migration through the vascular endothelium [28]. Furthermore, it inhibits the nucleotide-binding domain, leucine-rich–containing family, pyrin domain–containing-3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, which reduces the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-1β, thus dampening systemic inflammation [29–31].

Recently, the ESC updated its guidelines, elevating the recommendation for low-dose colchicine (0.5 mg daily) to class IIa (Level of Evidence: A) for reducing the risk of MI, stroke, and revascularization in patients with CCS and atherosclerotic CAD [32]. Similarly, the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) recommends colchicine for pericarditis after MI with a class IIb recommendation (Level of Evidence: C) [3]. However, the findings of the CLEAR SYNERGY trial did not support broader cardiovascular use of colchicine in ACS, raising questions about its efficacy in this setting.

Regarding all-cause mortality, stroke, and recurrent MI, our findings are consistent with those of Younas et al. While their meta-analysis included 7,161 patients, it incorporated trials with short-term or preprocedural colchicine administration, introducing clinical heterogeneity [33]. In contrast, our meta-analysis focused exclusively on post-MI patients treated with colchicine for at least one month, providing more robust and clinically relevant insights into its long-term benefits and risks. Additoinaly, the reported increase in adverse cardiovascular events in study of Younas et al. may stem from varying definitions across studies, which limits comparability [33]. In terms of stroke and revascularization, our findings contrast with those of the meta-analysis of Bao et al., which reported significant reductions with colchicine [34]. In our updated analysis, although the point estimates similarly favored colchicine, we did not observe statistically significant effects on the incidence of revascularization or stroke.

Compared to the meta-analyses by d’Entremont et al. [35] and Abdelaziz et al. [36], which included mixed populations of stable CAD, ACS, and stroke, our study focused exclusively on patients with ACS. While those broader analyses reported significant reductions in MACE largely driven by benefits in stable CAD patients, our ACS-only analysis of 11 RCTs found no significant reductions in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, or MACE. Earlier trials such as COLCOT and LoDoCo 2 showed colchicine’s benefit, particularly in stable CAD patients. COLCOT demonstrated a 23% relative reduction in cardiovascular death, recurrent MI, stroke, and urgent hospitalization, while LoDoCo 2 reported a 31% reduction in primary outcomes [37, 38]. In contrast, the lack of benefit seen in CLEAR SYNERGY, which focused primarily on patients with acute STEMI, suggests that colchicine’s efficacy may be limited to more stable patient populations [14]. These findings indicate that while colchicine may offer modest cardiovascular protection in CCS, it does not appear to confer similar benefits in the context of ACS.

Several factors may explain CLEAR SYNERGY’s neutral results [14]. First, it was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, but their own sensitivity analyses indicated no significant effect of the pandemic on outcomes. Second, colchicine dosing was modified mid-trial, and high treatment discontinuation (~ 26%) in both arms likely reduced power. Third, the trial enrolled mostly younger, predominantly male patients with lower cardiovascular risk, which may limit generalizability. Finally, timing and duration of colchicine therapy differed from earlier positive trials, raising pharmacological concerns. Due to its large sample size, CLEAR SYNERGY heavily influenced pooled meta-analytic results, potentially skewing findings toward the null.

From a practical standpoint, colchicine’s pharmacokinetic properties pose additional challenges. Its narrow therapeutic index, dependence on renal function for clearance, and metabolism via CYP3A4 and p-glycoprotein pathways make it susceptible to drug-drug interactions and toxicities [39]. This necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring, especially in individuals with advanced renal disease or concurrent use of interacting medications. CLEAR SYNERGY trial found a significantly higher incidence of GI adverse events, particularly diarrhea, in the colchicine group compared to placebo [14]. Although GI adverse events were not significantly increased overall, higher colchicine doses (1 mg daily) were associated with a significantly greater risk. The high heterogeneity may stem from varying definitions across studies, with some including only severe events. Notably, excluding the Tardif trial revealed a significant association, suggesting study-level differences (e.g., dose, reporting) contributed to the variability.

Our meta-analysis demonstrates notable strengths. First, it incorporates a robust sample size, including 11 studies with a total of 12,730 patients. Second, our focus on ACS patients, rather than the broader category of all CAD cases, allows for more specific insights into this population. Including subgroup analyses adds further depth to our findings and ensures a more nuanced understanding of the data.

Despite its strengths, our study has some limitations. Some studies included in the analysis may have lacked sufficient follow-up durations to capture long-term benefits. The CLEAR SYNERGY trial contributed significantly to the overall weight of the meta-analysis, which may have disproportionately influenced the conclusions. Additionally, moderate to high heterogeneity was observed in GI adverse events, MACE, and revascularization potentially affecting the generalizability of our findings. Variability in MACE in the definition of composite outcomes such as MACE may have affected results. Although sensitivity analyses were performed, this remains a limitation in comparing outcomes across studies. The inclusion of CRP as a variable was limited due to its omission in some studies and the unclear timing of sampling (e.g., peak levels versus other time points) in others, precluding its analysis in this meta-analysis. Additionally, although we conducted subgroup analyses by colchicine dose and treatment duration, we were unable to explore differences between ACS subtypes such as STEMI versus NSTEMI due to a lack of stratified outcome data in the included studies. This limitation should be considered when interpreting the applicability of our findings to specific patient subgroups.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This meta-analysis of 11 RCTs demonstrates that colchicine provides no significant clinical benefit in patients with ACS. It did not reduce all-cause or cardiovascular mortality, MI, stroke, revascularization, or MACE significantly. While earlier trials suggested potential benefit, these findings were not supported by larger, more recent studies. Colchicine was associated with a trend toward increased GI adverse events, particularly at higher doses. These results do not support the routine use of colchicine in ACS, underscoring the need for further research to better define its role, optimal patient selection, and therapeutic context.
